interview_metadata.name: Rickey Barham
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Sure, well, I grew up right here in Amsterdam, New York — born in 1994, only child, in a little ranch house off Route 30 on the edge of town. My dad worked at the old Beech-Nut plant before it moved out, and my mom did medical billing at St. Mary's. Pretty quiet childhood, honestly. I spent a lot of time in the garage with my dad taking apart whatever was broken — toasters, a busted lawnmower, an old GE refrigerator from my grandma's basement. That's really where the appliance stuff started. We weren't rich but we never went without, and there was always a project on the workbench. I went to Amsterdam High School, was decent at math and shop, kind of average at everything else. I was a worrier as a kid, still am — used to lie awake stressing about quizzes. After high school I started at Fulton-Montgomery Community College, did my associate's in electrical technology, finished in 2014. Right out of school I got hired at a regional appliance service company doing in-home repair, and I've basically been doing that ever since, about eleven years now. The biggest event was probably losing my dad in 2018 — heart attack, sudden, he was only 59. That really shook me up and pushed me into therapy for a while and into hiking, honestly, just to get out of my own head. I've never been married, no kids. I've had a couple of long-ish relationships but nothing that stuck. Right now I'm focused on saving up to open my own shop — sustainable appliance repair, retrofits, that kind of thing. My mom still lives in town, I see her every Sunday.

follow_ups.question: What was your favorite project from the garage days with your dad?
follow_ups.response: We rebuilt a 1970s Maytag wringer washer that we found at a yard sale for ten bucks. Took us almost a whole summer. Dad insisted on doing it without buying new parts unless we absolutely had to. Honestly, that's where I learned to actually read a wiring diagram instead of just guessing.

follow_ups.question: How did losing your dad change the direction of your life?
follow_ups.response: It made me serious about my own health, for one — I started hiking the High Peaks the next summer just to force myself outdoors. And it made me impatient about the business idea. Dad always said he'd open his own shop someday and never did. I don't want to be 59 still talking about it.

follow_ups.question: Are you close with your mom?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, very. She's 64 now, still in the same house. I do her appliance maintenance, she feeds me Sunday dinner. It's a fair trade.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, definitely. When I was 19, second semester at FMCC, I almost dropped out. I was working part-time at a Lowe's appliance section, making decent money, and a manager there offered to push me into an assistant manager track. My family was leaning that direction — steady paycheck, benefits. But one of my instructors, a guy named Mr. Petrarca, basically pulled me aside and said, 'You're going to regret this in ten years. Retail will eat you alive. Finish the degree.' I sat with it for about a week, talked to my dad, who actually surprised me by saying go with the degree. I turned the Lowe's thing down, finished the program, and that's how I ended up in service tech work instead of retail. If I'd taken that other path I think I'd be miserable in some district manager role right now.

follow_ups.question: Have you stayed in touch with Mr. Petrarca?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I send him a Christmas card every year and I had coffee with him at the Sunny Side Up diner last fall. He's retired now but still tinkers.

follow_ups.question: What was it about retail that scared you off?
follow_ups.response: The hours, mostly. And the fact that you don't actually fix anything — you just sell stuff and manage schedules. I need to end the day with something concretely repaired.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: That one was a conscious choice. I'm a planner — I made a literal pros-and-cons list in a spiral notebook. I still have it, actually. The 'finish degree' column had twice as many items.

follow_ups.question: Do you still make pros-and-cons lists for big decisions?
follow_ups.response: All the time. Probably to a fault. My ex used to make fun of me for it.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Honestly the school's career counseling office could've been better — Mr. Petrarca was a one-off. If FMCC had a real mentor program I think a lot of guys I knew wouldn't have dropped out. That's actually part of why I mentor junior techs now.

follow_ups.question: How many junior techs are you mentoring currently?
follow_ups.response: Two — a kid named Devon who's about a year in, and Marisol who started last fall.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: No partner right now, no kids. The most important family member is my mom, Linda. She's 64, retired from the medical billing job two years ago, lives about fifteen minutes from me on the south side of Amsterdam. I see her every Sunday — usually I bring groceries or fix something around the house, she makes a roast or a casserole. My dad, Wayne, passed in 2018 like I mentioned. I have an aunt and uncle in Gloversville, Aunt Bev and Uncle Ray, who I see at holidays. Ray is the one who got me into hiking, actually — he was a Adirondack 46er. I have two cousins on that side, Brian and Erica. Brian's a contractor in Schenectady, Erica moved to North Carolina years ago. On my dad's side it's thinner — his parents are both gone and he was the only kid. So really my close family is mom, then Bev and Ray, then Brian. That's the inner circle.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk to your mom during the week, not just Sunday?
follow_ups.response: She calls me Tuesday and Thursday evenings, pretty much like clockwork. Five minute chats usually. If I miss one she leaves a voicemail asking if I'm alive.

follow_ups.question: Have you been in any serious relationships recently?
follow_ups.response: I dated someone named Hannah for about two and a half years — she was a vet tech in Glens Falls. We broke up about eighteen months ago, partly the commute, partly we wanted different things on kids. Nothing serious since.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I think that's everyone. No siblings, no step-family. Pretty small tree.

follow_ups.question: Was being an only child something you liked or wished was different?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. Liked the attention as a kid, missed having backup as a teenager. Now I just wish my mom had another kid to share the worrying with.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yeah, a handful. My closest friend is Marcus — we went to FMCC together, he's an electrician now in Johnstown. We play guitar together once a week, usually Wednesdays at his place. There's the Glens Falls Trail Runners group, maybe ten people I see regularly on Saturday runs, and a couple of guys from that, Pete and Dave, I'd call real friends. There's also a photography meetup that gathers at the Albany Museum of Art quarterly — Joelle organizes it, she's a librarian, smart as hell. And Mrs. Kowalski, my elderly neighbor, who I do tech tutoring for and who I've kind of unofficially adopted as a grandma figure. So between Marcus, the trail runners, Joelle's photo group, and Mrs. K, that's my chosen family.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Marcus usually play on guitar?
follow_ups.response: He's a bluegrass guy, I'm more into the acoustic singer-songwriter stuff — Nick Drake, Iron and Wine, that Milk Carton Kids harmony stuff. We meet in the middle on John Prine and old Gillian Welch tunes.

follow_ups.question: How did you meet Joelle?
follow_ups.response: She was at one of my first gallery openings I attended in Albany, three years ago — we both got stuck looking at the same Salgado print for like ten minutes and started talking.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in a small two-bedroom apartment on Market Street, the upper unit of a converted Victorian, basically downtown Amsterdam. It's walking distance to the Mohawk Valley Heritage Area trail along the river and to a couple of decent coffee places — Russo's is my morning spot. The neighborhood is mixed — older retirees, some young families, a few college-age renters. Amsterdam's an old mill town that's been struggling for decades but lately there's been a real attempt to revitalize, especially around the Riverlink and the pedestrian bridge. There's still vacant storefronts on Main, but there's also a craft brewery and a new bakery that opened last year. I like the mix of decay and possibility, honestly — it's good photography territory.

follow_ups.question: What's your favorite spot in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: The pedestrian bridge over the Mohawk at sunrise. Especially in fall. I've shot probably 300 frames from that bridge.

follow_ups.question: How long have you lived in this apartment?
follow_ups.response: About four years. Moved in spring 2022 after Hannah and I started getting serious — though I ended up keeping it after we split.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. There's some petty theft and you hear about an overdose now and then on the police scanner, but in general it's quiet. I don't walk through the park after midnight, but I don't really need to.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, the landlord lives downstairs and across the street is Mrs. Kowalski. I know most folks on the block by face at least.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Ups are the affordability, the access to the Adirondacks, the slower pace. Downs are mostly economic — there's not a lot of high-end clientele here for the kind of business I want to build, so I have to travel out to Saratoga or Albany for the premium retrofit jobs. And winters are long.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever think about leaving Amsterdam?
follow_ups.response: I think about it about once a February. But my mom's here and my customer base is here. So no, not seriously.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Just me. I live alone in the apartment. There's a cat — her name is Solder, like the tin-lead kind, she's a six-year-old tortoiseshell I adopted from the Montgomery County SPCA. But she doesn't pay rent.

follow_ups.question: How long have you lived alone?
follow_ups.response: Since Hannah moved out in late 2023. About a year and a half now.

follow_ups.question: Do you like living alone?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes. I keep things very organized and it's nice to come home to silence after a noisy day of service calls. Sometimes lonely in February.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Permanent — just me and the cat.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My cousin Brian crashes on the couch maybe twice a year when he's doing a job near Amsterdam. That's about it.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Pretty structured. Monday through Friday I work, dispatch starts at 7:30 — I'm usually on my first call by 8:15. I'll do four to six service calls a day depending on how complicated. Tuesdays and Thursdays I have a standing 6 p.m. trail run with the group, weather permitting. Wednesdays Marcus and I play guitar. Saturday morning is the long trail run, 8 to 10 a.m., then I usually do errands, maybe a maker space afternoon. Sunday is mom day — I'm at her place by noon, home by 5, then I prep for the week. Sunday night I do meal prep and I lay out my schematics and parts list for Monday's calls.

follow_ups.question: What does meal prep look like for you?
follow_ups.response: I batch cook on Sunday. Usually a grain — farro or brown rice — a roasted vegetable tray, and one protein. This week was miso-glazed salmon. I portion it into glass containers for lunches.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually get up?
follow_ups.response: 5:45 weekdays. 6:30 on Saturdays. Sunday I let myself sleep till 7:30, which feels decadent.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I'm a home appliance repair technician at Mohawk Valley Appliance Service — we're a regional company, about twelve techs, based in Amsterdam but we cover everything from Schenectady to Utica. I work Monday through Friday, 7:30 to about 5:30 typically, with on-call rotation about every six weeks for weekend emergencies. I specialize in vintage and high-end appliances and increasingly in smart-home retrofits — putting modern controls on legacy machines. On the side I take maybe one or two private retrofit consultations a month, kind of pilot work for the business I want to launch.

follow_ups.question: What was your last interesting service call?
follow_ups.response: Last Thursday — a 1962 GE Stratoliner range that an interior designer in Saratoga wanted retrofitted with smart thermostat controls. Took me about six hours, two visits. Beautiful machine.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I volunteer one Saturday afternoon a month at the Amsterdam Senior Center doing tech tutoring — helping folks set up smartphones, smart thermostats, video calls with grandkids. I also serve on the safety committee at work, which means a monthly meeting and the occasional incident review. And I run my mom's snowblower and lawnmower maintenance, which isn't a chore exactly but it's standing.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been doing the senior center volunteering?
follow_ups.response: About three years. Started after one of my customers, a 78-year-old widow, broke down crying because she couldn't figure out her new thermostat. I figured I could help with that more systematically.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: A couple. I started lifting on Monday and Friday mornings before work — bought a used squat rack off Marketplace in March. I also dropped my evening scrolling — I deleted Instagram off my phone in February because I was losing an hour every night. Replaced it with reading; right now I'm on a Wendell Berry kick. And I added the second mentee, Marisol, so my work day has more teaching built into it.

follow_ups.question: Has cutting Instagram changed anything else?
follow_ups.response: I sleep better and I'm less twitchy. I still keep it on my laptop for the photography accounts I follow, but the phone version was killing me.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I don't have kids, so this one's a pass for me.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Pretty minimal. I've been pulled over twice that I can think of — once for a busted taillight on Route 5S, once doing 38 in a 30 in Johnstown. Both times got off with a warning. I've called the police once when a neighbor's apartment got broken into and they were responsive. That's about the extent of it.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel about the local police?
follow_ups.response: Generally okay. Amsterdam PD has its issues but the officers I've interacted with personally have been fine. I know that's not universal.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Honestly nothing else really stands out. Maybe being on a service call once when the customer was getting served with something — that was awkward but it wasn't really my interaction.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: Nobody close. A guy I went to high school with did time for distribution back around 2016 — sad story, he was a good kid. But not anyone in my circle now.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in every presidential and most midterms. Local elections I'm honestly hit or miss — I voted in the last Amsterdam mayoral but I missed a school board one a couple years back that I felt guilty about. I try to do absentee for the smaller ones now so I don't forget.

follow_ups.question: Did you vote in the 2024 election?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I did. In person, on the way to a service call actually.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd call myself a moderate independent who leans Democratic, especially on environmental and labor stuff. I grew up in a household that was sort of casually Republican — my dad was a union guy at Beech-Nut but voted Republican for cultural reasons mostly. I drifted left in community college, mostly because of the climate and energy stuff — that connected directly to what I was learning about efficiency standards. I'm not ideological. I like a balanced budget but I think trickle-down is nonsense. I think small business needs more support, but I also think we need real healthcare reform — being self-employed someday and trying to figure out coverage is genuinely scary. I'm pro-union, pro-environmental regulation, pro-gun rights to a moderate degree — I own a deer rifle. I'm wary of social media-driven outrage on both sides. Mostly I want competent, technocratic governance that takes climate seriously.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics much with your mom?
follow_ups.response: Carefully. She's still pretty conservative. We agree on local stuff, we tiptoe around national. We mostly just don't watch the news together.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've gotten more skeptical of big platforms — not just left or right policy stuff, but skeptical of how news gets filtered. I used to listen to a lot of cable news in the truck, now I mostly listen to longer-form podcasts and a couple of newsletters. I've also gotten more locally focused. National politics feels like a circus, but local stuff — zoning, the riverfront development, broadband expansion — that actually changes my life. So I've shifted attention there.

follow_ups.question: Which podcasts and newsletters?
follow_ups.response: I listen to Ezra Klein, The Daily, and a trade podcast called Service Industry Now. For newsletters I subscribe to Heather Cox Richardson and a regional one called the New York Focus.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat. I'm a white guy in a mostly white town so the day-to-day impact on me has been limited. But I read a lot during 2020 — Isabel Wilkerson, Ta-Nehisi Coates, some others — and it changed how I think about a bunch of stuff. I won't pretend I'm out marching, but I've donated to local groups, I've had hard conversations with my uncle, and I've thought a lot about how race shapes the customer base I see and don't see. Most of my high-end retrofit clients are white. That's worth noticing.

follow_ups.question: Which book hit you hardest?
follow_ups.response: Caste by Wilkerson. The framing of caste rather than just race let me see the patterns differently.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the basic claim — that policing falls harder on Black Americans and that needs to be fixed — is just empirically true. I don't agree with every tactic or every policy proposal that's gotten attached to the movement. I'm wary of defund as a slogan because I think it muddied what was actually a reasonable conversation about reallocation. But I think accountability, body cams, training reform — those are all good and I'd support tax dollars going there.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think we've gone through a real backlash cycle since 2020. There was a real opening for change and then a lot of it got pulled back, especially around schools and DEI stuff in workplaces. I don't think the answer is shouting matches, but I do think pretending the history isn't there is a worse answer. I try to keep reading and listening and not to be reactive.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I've had conversations with family and friends — careful ones — and I've donated. I went to one rally in Schenectady in summer 2020. I haven't joined anything ongoing.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Mixed bag. Marcus is on the same page as me, maybe a little to the left. Joelle has been the most actively engaged — she runs antiracist book groups at her library. My mom rolls her eyes at most of it but isn't hostile. My uncle Ray is more skeptical and we've had a couple of tense Thanksgivings.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Generally pretty good for 31. I'm active — hike, run, lift. My main thing is anxiety, which I've dealt with most of my life and which got worse after my dad died. I'm on a low-dose SSRI, sertraline 50 mg, prescribed by my primary at Saint Mary's, and I see a therapist about twice a month — Diane, in Schenectady. I have mild seasonal allergies, occasional lower back issues from crouching into appliance cavities all day, otherwise no chronic stuff.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been on sertraline?
follow_ups.response: Since late 2018, so about seven and a half years. Started a few months after dad. Tried to come off it once in 2022 and it didn't go well, so my doctor and I agreed to stay.

follow_ups.question: Do you do anything specific for the back issues?
follow_ups.response: Yeah — daily mobility routine, ten minutes morning and night, a foam roller, and I see a chiropractor maybe four times a year.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy parts: I have employer-provided health insurance through work, I have time to exercise, I can afford decent food. Hard parts: winter is brutal for outdoor exercise, the job is physically rough on knees and back, and I'm the kind of guy who has to consciously schedule the gym or it doesn't happen.

follow_ups.question: What's your insurance like through work?
follow_ups.response: Blue Cross HMO. Reasonable copays, decent network. It'd be one of the scariest things to give up when I go independent.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: I sprained my ankle pretty badly in October 2024 on a hike in the Sewards — slipped on wet leaves. Took about eight weeks to fully recover. Also had a panic attack in March of last year that landed me in urgent care because I thought it was cardiac. Turned out to just be stress plus too much coffee. That actually pushed me to be more disciplined about caffeine and to see Diane more regularly.

follow_ups.question: How much coffee do you drink now?
follow_ups.response: One pour-over in the morning, sometimes a small one around noon. I used to have four or five cups in the truck through the day.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: The ankle did — I was on modified duty for about three weeks, mostly shop work, no climbing into kitchens. My anxiety has occasionally cost me a sick day here or there. Otherwise no.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yeah, my mom had a knee replacement in spring 2024. I took two weeks off work to be her primary support during recovery. It went smoothly but it was eye-opening — she's getting older, she's alone, and at some point caring for her will be the dominant thing in my life. I've started thinking about that.

follow_ups.question: Have you and your mom talked about long-term plans?
follow_ups.response: We had one good conversation last summer about it. She's adamant she's not leaving the house. We agreed I'd help her stay in it as long as it's safe.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I've been lucky on access. My primary is great, Dr. Patel at Saint Mary's. Wait times for therapy are the biggest issue — I waited four months to start with Diane back in 2018, and a friend who needed mental health care recently waited even longer. I haven't really forgone care, but I've delayed a dental thing because the copay was nasty.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: I see a chiropractor for the back stuff, and I've done acupuncture maybe a half dozen times — found it helpful for stress. I take a fish oil and a vitamin D in winter. Nothing too exotic. My mom is a believer in apple cider vinegar for everything; I am not.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I drink moderately. Maybe two or three beers on a weekend, a glass of bourbon on a Friday after a hard week. I went through a heavier period right after my dad died — closer to a few drinks every night for maybe six months — and Diane and I worked through that. Now I'm careful. I don't smoke anything.

follow_ups.question: What's your go-to beer?
follow_ups.response: Anything from Druthers in Saratoga, but I'm partial to Common Roots Out of Bounds.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: Just the sertraline, prescribed. I've tried marijuana edibles maybe three or four times in my life — most recently at a friend's place in Burlington maybe two years ago. Wasn't really for me, made me anxious actually, which is the opposite of what people promise. No pain meds beyond ibuprofen.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I'm on employer insurance, so my out-of-pocket is mostly therapy copays and the occasional urgent care visit. My mom is on Medicare and a supplement, which has been okay. The knee replacement was a strain financially but she had savings. We're managing.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm a believer. I got all my COVID shots including boosters, get a flu shot every fall, I'm up to date on tetanus because of the job. My doctor recommended an HPV catch-up last year and I did it.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Dr. Patel first. CDC website second. The NYT health section. I also follow a couple of physician-scientists on Substack — Katelyn Jetelina's Your Local Epidemiologist mainly.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Overall steady, with some peaks and valleys. The breakup with Hannah is fully in the rearview now and I feel good about being on my own. Work is going well — I got a raise in January and the retrofit side projects are picking up momentum. The business planning is exciting and stressful at the same time. There's a low-grade hum of anxiety about the future, especially around healthcare and money if I go independent. But day to day I'd say I'm content. I sleep okay, I look forward to the small stuff — running, Sunday dinner, guitar with Marcus.

follow_ups.question: What's been the high point of the year so far?
follow_ups.response: A four-day solo trip to Acadia in April. Just me, my camera, a notebook, a lot of fog and shoreline. Came back clearer.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last November, around the anniversary of my dad's death — it always hits me weirdly around then. I had a stretch of about two weeks where I wasn't sleeping well, was snippy with coworkers, lost interest in everything I usually like. Diane and I talked it through, I leaned harder on Marcus, I went up to Crane Mountain alone one Saturday and sat on the summit for about an hour. By Thanksgiving I was on the other side of it. But it was real.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: Generalized anxiety disorder, formally diagnosed in 2018. Some depressive episodes layered on, especially around the November anniversary. Medicated and in therapy, like I mentioned. It's part of who I am, I've made peace with that.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My mom has her own grief and her own quiet sadness, but she handles it through routine and church. She's never seen a therapist and I don't think she will. We talk about dad sometimes but not deeply.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I was raised Methodist — my mom still goes to First United Methodist on Division Street. I went through confirmation, the whole thing. In my early twenties I drifted away and would call myself agnostic now, with a soft spirituality around nature. The Adirondacks are basically my church. I do still occasionally go to a Christmas Eve service with my mom, and I find the rituals meaningful even if the doctrine doesn't land for me. I don't pray in a formal sense but I do something close to it when I'm on a summit or shooting at dawn — a kind of attention or gratitude. I'm respectful of religion generally, suspicious of organized political religion specifically.

follow_ups.question: Does your mom mind that you've drifted?
follow_ups.response: She used to push gently. She's stopped. I think she figures I'll come back eventually or I won't, either way I'm a good person.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I'm a light user. I have Facebook mostly for my mom's generation — that's how I see updates from extended family and how I get invited to the Glens Falls Trail Runners events. Instagram I dropped from my phone like I mentioned, but I use it on desktop to follow photographers and a few makers. I have a small public Instagram for my own photography — about 800 followers, mostly other industrial-photography people. No TikTok, no Twitter, no Threads. Reddit occasionally for appliance repair forums and r/AppliancesUnderRepair specifically, where I sometimes answer questions.

follow_ups.question: What's your photography Instagram handle?
follow_ups.response: It's @barham.silvergelatin. Mostly black and white industrial stuff.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: Not really. I lean on Marcus, Diane, and trail running. I might post a moody photo when I'm in a funk but I'm not going to Facebook to crowdsource feelings.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: Stress is up modestly because of the business planning. Coping is better than it used to be — more exercise, less drinking, less doomscrolling, more reading and therapy. Net result is probably better wellbeing than two years ago despite more stressors.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: Just me. And the cat, Solder.

transcript.response: No.

transcript.response: No.

transcript.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Just me, 100 percent.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Rent — $1,250. Truck payment, $389. Groceries around $400. Gas and insurance combined another $350 ish. Therapy copays maybe $120. Student loan, $185. That's most of the big stuff.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: About $3,200 last month, which is pretty typical. Sometimes it jumps to $4,000 if there's a tool purchase or a trip. I track it in a spreadsheet.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: Rent. $1,250 a month, no utilities included. I've thought about buying — there's some affordable stuff in Amsterdam — but I'm holding cash for the business launch.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Winter heating is brutal — National Grid bill can hit $280 in January versus $90 in May. Holidays are an extra $400 or so in December for gifts and travel to Brian's. Hiking gear in the spring is another seasonal bump — boots last fall were $230. Summer photography trips add up. Tax refund usually hits around early April and I throw most of it at the business fund.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: Just budgeted ahead. I have a sinking fund for known seasonal bumps and an emergency fund for surprises. Used the sinking fund for the snow tires last November.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm a saver. High-yield savings at Marcus by Goldman for the emergency fund — about $11,000 right now, which is roughly four months of expenses. A separate savings labeled 'business launch' that's around $18,000. 401k at work that I contribute to up to the match, plus a Roth IRA I max out. I'm pretty disciplined.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: Both. The business fund is the big target — I want $35,000 before I quit my job, to cover equipment, insurance, and six months of runway. The emergency fund is the rainy day. Retirement is the long horizon.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: Student loan, federal, $185 a month, about $9,000 left. Truck loan, $389 a month, about $14,000 left. One credit card I use for points and pay off every month — no carried balance. That's it.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: Not really. I've delayed wants — a new lens I've been eyeing for a year, a guitar I want — but nothing necessary has gone unpaid. I'm aware that's a privileged position.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Home appliance repair technician. Day to day I drive a service van to customer homes — refrigerators, washers, dryers, dishwashers, ovens, ranges, wine coolers, occasional small commercial gear. I diagnose using multimeters and manufacturer diagnostic software, order parts, do the repair, document the service call, handle the invoicing. Increasingly I do smart-home retrofit consults — putting modern controls and energy monitoring on older or vintage appliances. I also mentor two junior techs and serve on our safety committee. Important duties: accurate diagnostics, parts inventory management, customer communication, safety code adherence, and documentation.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: No, not unionized. We're a private regional company. There's a national trade association — the United Servicers Association — I'm a member but it's not a union.

transcript.response: All 52.

transcript.response: Around 45 most weeks, 50-55 on on-call rotation weeks.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: Yes.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Sort of — the side retrofit consults I treat as a registered LLC, so technically yes. Two jobs.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: Two — the main W-2 job and the LLC. I did two retrofit consults last month.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: From the main job, about $4,200 net after taxes and 401k. From the LLC, about $850 last month from two consults. Around $5,050 total take-home.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: Biweekly from the main job. The LLC payments come whenever the customer pays.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: About $5,050 net. Gross is around $6,700, annualized to roughly $80,000.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, filed electronically through TurboTax in late February. Got a refund of about $1,800 which I put into the business fund.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job?
transcript.response: Eleven years this fall. Benefits are solid — Blue Cross HMO, dental, vision, 401k with a 4% match, three weeks PTO, paid certifications. It's a good package.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?
transcript.response: Good. My boss Gary has been there 20 years, we get along, he gives me autonomy. The other techs are like brothers — we eat lunch in the shop on Wednesdays. The mentees look up to me, which is rewarding.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: Day-to-day is predictable — dispatch is set the evening before, occasional emergency add-ons. On-call weekends are the wild card. Flexibility is moderate — I can usually swap a day off with another tech if I need it, and Gary is reasonable about doctor or therapy appointments.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: Not applicable — no kids.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No, nothing like that.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: There was a stretch in February — slow month, fewer service calls, no LLC consults — where the side income was basically zero. Nothing dramatic, I just leaned more on the main paycheck and skipped that month's transfer to the business fund.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: I'd put it on the credit card and pay it off from the emergency fund the next day. Wouldn't blink. That's exactly what the emergency fund is for.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: Good, with some anxiety about the future. Right now I'm secure — savings, retirement contributions, manageable debt, decent income for the area. The anxiety is all about the leap to self-employment. I know the numbers, I've modeled it, I have a runway, but actually leaving the W-2 paycheck is going to be terrifying. I tell myself I'm doing the right things — slow, careful, well-capitalized. That's about all I can do.

transcript.response: Independent, leaning Democrat. I'd say moderately strong on the lean — I've voted Democrat in every presidential since 2016 — but I'm not a party loyalist and I've voted for Republican local candidates I respected.

transcript.response: Democratic Party, currently.

transcript.response: Associate's degree in business administration from FMCC.

transcript.response: Yes — full time throughout my childhood.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: Medical billing specialist. She coded patient visits, submitted insurance claims, handled denials and appeals, managed accounts receivable for a primary care practice. She was meticulous — clearly where I get it.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: A small primary care medical practice in Amsterdam, three or four doctors. Outpatient family medicine.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, the whole time.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: He was a maintenance welder and millwright at the Beech-Nut food processing plant — kept the production lines running, fabricated and repaired equipment, did preventive maintenance. After Beech-Nut closed the local plant he transitioned to a similar role at a Schenectady manufacturer until his death.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: Beech-Nut was a baby food and snack food manufacturer — they made jarred baby food, fruit pouches, and Beech-Nut gum. The later job was a steel fabrication shop in Schenectady.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: Five years out — I want to be running my own shop, Mohawk Valley Sustainable Appliance, with one or two employees and a steady book of retrofit clients across the Capital Region. I want to have my Master Technician status, be a regular speaker at the regional trade shows, and have a small product line of retrofit kits for vintage machines. Personally I want to own a small house in or near Amsterdam, maybe up toward Galway, with a real workshop. I want to be partnered again — I miss having that — and open to kids if it goes that way, but at peace if it doesn't. I want my mom healthy and still in her house. I want to have done a real trip to Iceland or Japan by then. I want to still be playing guitar with Marcus on Wednesdays.

follow_ups.question: Iceland or Japan first?
follow_ups.response: Iceland first — I want to shoot the geothermal landscape. Japan is the bigger trip, I'd save that for later.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Three things, in order. First, integrity — doing the job right whether anyone's watching or not, telling customers the honest answer even if it costs me the sale. Second, the people I love — my mom, my closest friends, a future partner if I'm lucky. Third, curiosity — the feeling of figuring something out, whether it's an obscure motor wiring problem or a new chord progression or a hike I haven't done. If I have those three things I think the rest sorts itself out.

summaries.behavioral_economist: Rickey is a textbook planner with a low risk tolerance: he maintains separate sinking, emergency, business-launch, and retirement buckets, tracks every dollar in a spreadsheet, holds ~4 months of expenses liquid, and would cover a $400 shock without blinking (Q57, Q61, Q62, Q82). His time preference skews patient — he is willing to defer wants (lens, guitar, house) for years to over-capitalize before leaving a stable W-2 job for self-employment (Q63, Q64, Q83). Loss aversion shows up in his explicit fear about losing employer health insurance and his $35K target for business launch (Q32, Q62, Q83). He is responsive to mentor signaling (Petrarca's advice altered his career), forms identity-consistent habits (Sunday meal prep, weekly mentorship, monthly volunteering), and consciously curates incentive environments by deleting Instagram and reducing caffeine (Q02, Q15, Q17, Q18, Q33).
summaries.political_scientist: Rickey identifies as an independent who leans Democratic with moderate strength, votes reliably in presidential and most midterm elections, and has voted Democrat in every presidential since 2016 while still occasionally supporting Republican local candidates he respects (Q23, Q95, Q96). His policy profile is technocratic and pragmatic — pro-union (despite working non-union), pro-environmental regulation, moderate on gun rights (owns a deer rifle), supportive of healthcare reform driven by personal stakes, and skeptical of both left and right outrage cycles (Q24). He has shifted attention from national to local politics — riverfront development, broadband, zoning — reflecting high local civic attachment, reinforced by senior-center volunteering and the safety committee at work (Q17, Q25). Institutional trust is selective: high trust in personal physicians, CDC, and policy-analytical voices like Ezra Klein and Heather Cox Richardson; lower trust in cable news and social-media-mediated discourse (Q25, Q42).
summaries.psychologist: Rickey presents as conscientious and organized to a near-trait level (spreadsheets, schematic prep, parts inventory, planner-style decision-making) coexisting with elevated neuroticism — a self-described 'worrier' with formally diagnosed generalized anxiety disorder, depressive flares around anniversaries, and a history of medicated and therapy-supported management (Q03, Q15, Q31, Q44, Q45). His coping architecture is mature and multi-modal: SSRI + biweekly therapy, daily mobility work, exercise as mental reset, deliberate reduction of stimuli (Instagram, caffeine), and a stable rotation of restorative people and places (Marcus on Wednesdays, mom on Sundays, Adirondack summits, Acadia solo trips) (Q15, Q18, Q33, Q43, Q44, Q47). His identity hinges on the integration of precision (technician, methodical workflows) and creative expression (photography, guitar, retrofits) — the 'organized art-driven' self he names explicitly — and his motivational architecture is achievement-driven but anchored in care (mentees, mother, Mrs. Kowalski), suggesting a high-agreeableness, high-conscientiousness profile balanced by self-aware emotional vulnerability (Q07, Q17, Q35, Q109).
